title: Family & people
goal: Talk about your family, say whose something is, and say what or whom you have.
intro: Odia has a rich set of kinship words: it matters whether an uncle is on your mother's or father's side and whether a sibling is older or younger. In this unit you learn the genitive ending **-ର** ('s, of), the respectful **-ଙ୍କ**, how to say *I have*, and the plural endings **-ମାନେ** and **-ଗୁଡ଼ିକ**.

vocab.note: What most Odias actually call their mother.
Also used to address any young woman a little older than you. Cuttack also: ନାନୀ (nani).
Also a polite way to address a man a bit older than you.
Also a polite address for older women.
Father's elder brother: ବଡ଼ବାପା. Wife of ଦାଦା: ଖୁଡ଼ୀ (khuṛi).
Everyday: ବାହା ହୋଇଛି (baha hoichhi) 'has got married'.

phrases.en: Who is there in your family?
phrases.note: Doubling କିଏ asks for a list.

phrases.en: There are five people in my family.

phrases.native: ମୋର ଜଣେ ପୁଅ ଓ ଜଣେ ଝିଅ ଅଛନ୍ତି।
phrases.roman: morô jôṇe puô o jôṇe jhiô ôchhônti.
phrases.en: I have a son and a daughter.
Do you have brothers and sisters?
I'm the youngest in the family.
My elder sister studies at college.

grammar.title: Possessives: -ର and respectful -ଙ୍କ
grammar.body:
To say *X's* or *of X*, add **-ର** (*-rô*) to the noun: ଲିପିର ଭାଇ *Lipirô bhai* 'Lipi's brother'. With respected people (parents, elders, teachers) and with plurals, use **-ଙ୍କ** (*-ṅkô*) instead: ବାପାଙ୍କ ନାମ *bapaṅkô namô* 'Father's name', ପିଲାମାନଙ୍କ ବହି 'the children's books'.

Pronoun possessives (the final -ର is often dropped before a noun):
ମୋ(ର) my · ଆମ(ର) our · ତୋ(ର) your (intimate) · ତୁମ(ର) your (familiar) · ଆପଣଙ୍କ your (formal) · ତା(ର) his/her · ତାଙ୍କ his/her (respectful) · ସେମାନଙ୍କ their

'Whose?' is **କାହାର** (*kaharô*).

grammar.title: Saying 'I have': genitive + ଅଛି
grammar.body:
Odia has no verb 'to have'. Instead you say *of-me there-is*: the owner takes **-ର** (or ମୋର, ତୁମର…) and the verb is **ଅଛି** — or **ଅଛନ୍ତି** if what you have are people (respect!). The negative is **ନାହିଁ**.

ମୋର ଗୋଟିଏ ଗାଡ଼ି ଅଛି 'I have a car'; ମୋର ଭାଇ ନାହିଁ 'I don't have a brother'.

examples.native: ମୋର ଦୁଇ ଭାଇ ଓ ଜଣେ ଭଉଣୀ ଅଛନ୍ତି।
examples.roman: morô dui bhai o jôṇe bhôuṇi ôchhônti.
examples.en: I have two brothers and a sister.

grammar.title: Plurals and (no) gender
grammar.body:
Odia has **no grammatical gender** — no masculine/feminine nouns, and verbs and adjectives never change for gender. (A few Sanskrit words have separate female forms, like ଛାତ୍ର/ଛାତ୍ରୀ 'student m/f', but grammar doesn't care.)

Plurals: for **people** add **-ମାନେ** (*-mane*): ପିଲାମାନେ 'children', ସାଙ୍ଗମାନେ 'friends'. For **things and animals** add **-ଗୁଡ଼ିକ** (*-guṛikô*), colloquially **-ଗୁଡ଼ା** (*-guṛa*): ବହିଗୁଡ଼ିକ 'the books'. After a number or a word like ସବୁ 'all', no plural ending is needed: ଦୁଇ ଭାଇ 'two brothers'. In front of case endings, -ମାନେ becomes **-ମାନଙ୍କ** (ପିଲାମାନଙ୍କୁ 'to the children').

examples.en: He is a student, his sister is a student (f).

dialogue.title: The family photo
dialogue.setting: Lipi shows Sam a family photo on her phone.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ଏ ମୋ ବାପା, ଆଉ ଏ ମୋ ବୋଉ।
lines.roman: e mo bapa, au e mo bou.
lines.en: This is my dad, and this is my mum.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ସେ ମୋ ସାନ ଭାଇ ବାବୁ। ସେ ସ୍କୁଲରେ ପଢ଼େ।
lines.roman: se mo sanô bhai Babu. se skulôre pôṛhe.
lines.en: That's my little brother Babu. He's at school.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.en: Do you have an elder sister too?

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ହଁ। ଅପା ବିବାହିତ। ତାଙ୍କ ସ୍ୱାମୀ କଟକରେ ଚାକିରି କରନ୍ତି।
lines.roman: hôṃ. ôpa bibahitô. taṅkô swami Kôṭôkôre chakiri kôrônti.
lines.en: Yes. She's married. Her husband works in Cuttack.

lines.speaker: Lipi
lines.native: ମୋ ଜେଜେବାପା ଆଉ ଜେଜେମା। ସେମାନେ ଆମ ସହିତ ରହନ୍ତି।
lines.roman: mo jejebapa au jejema. semane amô sôhitô rôhônti.
lines.en: My grandfather and grandmother. They live with us.

culture: Odias rarely call older people by their first names. Instead they use kinship words — **ଭାଇନା** (elder brother), **ଅପା** (elder sister), **ମାଉସୀ** (auntie), **ଦାଦା** (uncle) — even for neighbours, shopkeepers and strangers. Respected relatives get respectful verb forms (ବାପା କ'ଣ କରନ୍ତି?). Many families are still *joint families* (ଯୌଥ ପରିବାର), with grandparents, parents and children under one roof.
